sections.COMMENTS:
ï»¿    **COMMENTS**
The southern Apennines between the Molise units and the region south of the Sources of the 23 November 1980 Irpinia earthquake (M 6.9) can be seen as a NE-dipping system of large seismogenic faults along the crest of the thrustbelt. Most of the major earthquakes that have been associated with some of these Sources have a magnitude ranging between 6.0 and 7.0. Although simplified, this view fairly well synthesizes what has been observed in the past few decades.
Out of the numerous catastrophic earthquakes that have hit the central and southern Apennines, some have been characterized not only by multiple, destructive events but also a by "distributed epicenters", i.e. shocks having occurred at dozens of km apart Ã� apparently at the very same moment. Together with the better studied 5-30 December 1456, the 9 September 1349 stands out for its puzzling epicentral locations and, given its age, the obstacles in locating a reliable and sufficiently vast historical documentation.
This seismic crisis includes 2-3 principal events, all (seemingly) having occurred on 9 September. One of these events (comparatively well documented) is located among the western Molise and south-eastern Lazio regions, with damage down to the Venafro Mts and the Venafro plain (M 6.6). This event had been predated by a foreshock (M 4.5) that had occurred on 22 January of the same year.
This Source is meant to explain the southern sub-event above, and follows the interpretation recently proposed by Galli and Naso (2009).
Although Guidoboni and Comastri (2005) reported that damage had been primarily felt in the localities of Venafro, Atina and Isernia, Galli and Naso (2009) report geological evidence (augmented by a geomorphological and historical analysis) of rupture episodes that, through absolute dating, they have associated with the 1349 earthquake. In particular, they have discovered the fracturing of a Roman aqueduct, whose location is in good agreement with the along-strike extents of the fault they have identified.
Although the historical catalogues indicate a Mw of 6.6 for this event, Galli and Naso (2009) have calculated a value of 6.5, based on their findings. We have opted for the latter value.
In synthesis, the length, strike, dip, and rake of this Source are based on the geological data from Galli and Naso (2009), while the width is calculated from the empirical relationships by Wells and Coppersmith (1994). Minimum and maximum depth are based on the occurrence of surface rupture (the former) and the width extents (the latter). The Mw derives from the work by Galli and Naso (2009).
sections.OPEN QUESTIONS:
1) Did this Source really cause the southern event of the 1349 multiple earthquake?
Or is the Source more to the west, where the macroseismic field is denser?
2) Is this Source the northern reach of the SW-dipping, seismogenic fault system?
3) If the above is true, does seismogenesis in the southern Apennines occur through a horst system on top of the thrustbelt? Or is this Source a singularity in the system?
sections.SUMMARIES:
Although the area has been hit by numerous, catastrophic earthquakes, few hypotheses concerning the 1349 multiple event have been proposed in the literature. In fact, Galli & Naso (2009) are the authors of the work that this Individual Source is mainly based upon.
Guidoboni and Comastri (2005)
Their work is an extensive review and analysis of a large amount of historical Sources (both previously known and unavailable) for all earthquakes that have occurred in Italy and the surrounding areas from the 11th to the 15th century.
They show the pattern of damage distribution that they obtained through a storiographic reconstruction. The macroseismic field they identified shows damage particularly in the south-eastern Lazio region, i.e. slightly to the W-NW with respect to the area of the Aquae Iuliae Source we present.
Galli and Naso (2009)
These authors have reappraised the effects of the 1349 earthquake, performed an interpretation of aerial photographs and a field survey, and have carried out paleoseismological analyses across a N130 normal fault that crosses the border between the Molise and Campania regions. In the view of the authors, this fault shows repeated ruptures during the late Holocene, constrained with paleoseismological trenches. The authors contend that the last rupture episode well fits the 1349 event, both in terms of the dating and the rupture dimension. They also maintain that their archaeo-seismic analyses have shown the rupture of a Roman aqueduct. The amount of displacement of the aqueduct across seems indicative of other faulting event(s) during the RomanÃ�High Middle-Age period. Therefore, the authors have tried to ascertain whether such latter rupture events could be associated with other major earthquakes in the area. They suggest the 346 AD or 848 AD as potential candidates, but they do not rule potentially unknown events.
